steps.text: That 0x1000 value is PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION, coming from lsm.dll via RPC — this is a typical benign pattern, but I should still verify the source process.

arguments.reasoning: Verify the svchost source process image path, command line, and user.
Verify the target is the genuine lsass.exe.

steps.text: That svchost instance started at boot with sequential GUID timestamps and minimal access, matching the expected lsm.dll call trace—this looks benign, so no need to dig further into lsass access.

submission.reasoning: I think this alert is benign. On workstation5, the genuine C:\windows\system32\svchost.exe (proc-531d458284) opened a handle to the genuine C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe (proc-84b00ee671) 6 times between 06:36:43 and 06:36:44 on 2020-10-23. The access it was granted was 0x1000 (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION). That right only lets a process query basic details; it cannot read lsass memory, so it can't be used to dump credentials. The call trace shows the request came from lsm.dll (the Local Session Manager service) through normal RPC handling (RPCRT4) to ntdll and KERNELBASE. It contains no unknown modules or injected code, and dumping tools like dbghelp/dbgcore don't appear. The two processes' IDs were created one after the other, which suggests svchost started at boot together with lsass. This is normal Windows session-management activity, not credential theft.
